claims.text: Cold spray additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi will reduce residual thermal stresses relative to laser powder bed fusion.
Cold spray additive manufacturing will preserve the intrinsic mechanical properties of AlCrFeNiSi relative to conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
The AlCrFeNiSi powder is produced by gas atomization.
The AlCrFeNiSi powder has a predominantly spherical morphology.
The AlCrFeNiSi powder particles have native oxide layers.
Cold spray uses supersonic gas flow to accelerate powder particles onto a substrate without melting them.
The proposed substrate-preheat temperature is below 200°C.
The proposed process applies to miniature features smaller than 5 mm.
Mechanical properties are to be tested at room temperature.
Achieving bonding without significant thermal input requires sufficient particle velocity governed by gas pressure and nozzle design.
Avoiding melting will retain the original powder microstructure with minimal grain growth.
Avoiding melting will minimize phase transformations.
Avoiding melting prevents the steep thermal gradients that generate residual stresses.
High-velocity particle impact produces mechanical interlocking and metallurgical bonding.
Cold-sprayed AlCrFeNiSi parts will have higher yield strength than laser-powder-bed-fused counterparts.
Cold-sprayed AlCrFeNiSi parts will have higher ductility than laser-powder-bed-fused counterparts.
Cold spray will reduce or eliminate the need for post-production heat treatment or stress relief.
Laser powder bed fusion produces significant thermal gradients and residual stresses in the baseline components.
Laser powder bed fusion causes microstructural changes in the baseline components.
The benefits may not translate to larger components because of scaling challenges and changes in particle–substrate dynamics.
